title: 7 Outlet Wiring Mistakes I Find in Almost Every Older House
reference_points: How To Home (RO6Kq65HwNw), in order: 1) hot/neutral on the wrong terminals (black to brass, white to silver, bare/green to green screw) = reverse polarity; 2) too much bare copper stripped (can touch ground/other conductors, arcing) or too little (insulation under the screw), use the strip gauge; 3) loop wrapped counterclockwise pushes wire out, clockwise pulls it in, worse with stranded wire; 4) backstab/push-in 'speed wiring' loosens with heat cycling and movement, wire can back out; 5) two wires under one terminal screw is against code, use pigtails; 6) tools: Phillips cams out, square/Robertson or combo bits tighten terminals better.
brief: Older houses collect years of receptacle work by previous owners, and seven faults come up again and again. 1) Backstabbed connections: push-in holes grip the wire with a small spring contact that can loosen as the device heats and cools, leading to heating and arcing; the UL listing limits push-in terminals to 14 AWG solid copper on 15 A circuits, and the side screws or screw-clamp back-wire terminals make a firmer connection. 2) Reversed polarity: black (hot) belongs on the brass screws, white (neutral) on the silver screws; reversed, the outlet still works but parts of plugged-in lamps and appliances meant to be neutral become live. A plug-in tester shows it. 3) A three-prong outlet on a two-wire circuit with no ground: NEC 406.4(D)(2) allows only a two-prong replacement, a GFCI receptacle marked 'No Equipment Ground', or a three-prong outlet fed from a GFCI and marked 'GFCI Protected' and 'No Equipment Ground'. 4) Bootleg ground: a jumper from neutral to the ground screw fools a three-light tester into reading correct, but puts current-carrying neutral on appliance metal, which becomes live if the neutral opens; the NEC prohibits it. 5) Two wires under one screw: terminals take one conductor unless identified for more; the fix is a pigtail. 6) Poor terminations: loops wrapped counterclockwise push out as the screw tightens; manufacturers specify about three-quarters of a turn clockwise, stripped to the device's strip gauge, with no insulation under the screw and no extra bare copper. 7) Aluminum branch wiring (homes wired roughly 1965-1973) on devices not marked CO/ALR; CPSC treats CO/ALR devices as only a partial fix and recognizes COPALUM or AlumiConn repairs at every connection, done by a licensed electrician. Power goes off at the breaker and is verified dead before any receptacle is touched; local code may differ.
sources: https://www.ecmweb.com/national-electrical-code/qa/article/20900802/stumped-by-the-code-nec-requirements-when-replacing-nongrounding-type-receptacles — 406.4(D)(2) three replacement options and markings

doubts: The bootleg-ground prohibition is commonly cited as NEC 250.142(B); I did not see the code text, so no article number is given. 'Find in almost every older house' is the title's voice only and has no survey data behind it. Reverse polarity: no NEC article number given (not verified). The reference's tool tip (Phillips vs square/combo bits) is not a 'mistake in older houses' and was left out. The aluminum-wiring date range is CPSC's; aluminum wiring is not limited to those years.

title: BEWARE of These 3 Common Wiring Mistakes on Outlets & Switches
reference_points: Silver Cymbal (irK7l3eyB8g, about 5 min): 1) wrong wire on the wrong terminal: silver = white/neutral, brass = black/hot; outlet still works but reverse polarity; check with a plug-in tester; 2) hook on backwards: the screw tightens clockwise, hook must face clockwise or it pushes out; plus stripping too much (bare copper sticks out, can short) or too little (insulation under the screw), he says 3/4 inch; 3) backstab/back-wiring holes give poor contact, electricians avoid them; bonus: screw-clamp back-wire outlets with a strip gauge and a pressure plate, more contact area, two wires per side; ground screw still needs a hook. Safety caveat at end.
brief: The same three faults turn up on receptacles and on switches. 1) Wrong wire on the wrong terminal. On a receptacle, brass screws take the black (hot) wire, silver screws the white (neutral) and the green screw the bare or green ground; swapped, it still works but reverse polarity leaves the shell of a lamp socket or an appliance's internal parts live when switched off. A plug-in tester shows it. On a switch, the switch must interrupt the hot conductor, never the neutral (NEC 404.2(B)); a switch on the neutral leaves the fixture live while it is off. On a switch loop wired with two-wire cable, the white conductor used as a hot must be re-marked with tape or paint (black or red) at every termination and visible point (NEC 200.7(C)(1)). On three-way switches, the darker 'common' screw takes the line or the load, not a traveler. 2) The hook formed the wrong way. Terminal screws tighten clockwise, so the loop goes clockwise about three-quarters of a turn; wrapped the other way it is pushed out from under the screw. Strip length follows the gauge molded on the device (Leviton specifies about 5/8 inch for side wiring): too much leaves bare copper that can touch the ground or the box, too little traps insulation under the screw and gives a poor, heating connection. 3) Backstabbing. Push-in holes hold the wire with a small spring contact that can loosen over time; on receptacles the UL listing limits them to 14 AWG solid copper on 15 A circuits. Better devices use screw-clamp back-wire terminals, which take solid or stranded wire, some taking two wires per terminal where the device is marked for it. Power is off at the breaker and verified dead with a tester first; local code may differ.
sources: https://forums.mikeholt.com/threads/white-conductor.58988/page-2 — 404.2(B) switch shall not disconnect grounded conductor; 200.7(C)(1) re-identification
https://www.ecmag.com/magazine/articles/article-detail/codes-standards-switching-neutral-ok — switch loop re-identified white used only as supply to the switch
https://inspectapedia.com/electric/Duplex-receptacle-install-instructions-Leviton.pdf — Leviton: loop clockwise 3/4 turn, 5/8 in strip for side wire, strip per gauge for back wire
https://leviton.com/content/dam/leviton/commercial-industrial/product_documents/instruction_sheet/PK-A3292-10-02-0A-W.pdf — Leviton instruction sheet, clockwise loop, strip length
https://forums.mikeholt.com/threads/ul-498-backstab-receptacles.41003/post-630172 — UL guide: push-in limited to 15 A, 14 AWG solid copper; screw-clamp back-wire OK for solid and stranded
https://iaeimagazine.org/standards/significant-changes-to-the-2023-nec-by-cmp-18/ — 2023 NEC push-in 14 AWG solid copper only
doubts: His transcript actually names four faults (polarity, hook direction, strip length, backstab); his strip-length point is part of the hook mistake, so I folded it into 2) to keep three. He says strip 3/4 inch; Leviton's sheets say about 5/8 inch, so the brief says follow the device's strip gauge. The UL 14 AWG solid-copper push-in limit was verified for receptacles; I did not verify the same wording for switches, so it is stated for receptacles only. Silver Cymbal's 'eight wires' on clamp outlets is device-specific (two per terminal only where marked). The three-way common-screw detail is standard practice, not checked against a manufacturer sheet in this round.

title: 10 Breaker Box Mistakes That Make a Panel Dangerous (Is Yours One?)
reference_points: LRN2DIY (NF4zxBAuRoI), in order: 1) missing/illegible circuit labels (circuit tracer tip); 2) overloading the panel (keep usage to about 80% of panel rating; tandems); 3) cables rubbing on knockouts without bushings/connectors; pause: call an electrician if unsure; 4) breaker too big for the wire (14 AWG 15 A, 12 AWG 20 A; white vs yellow NM); 5) improper grounding (cut main ground, twisted grounds with one pigtail); 6) two neutrals in one bus-bar hole; 7) wrong wire colors, re-mark a white used as hot with red tape; 8) double-tapped breakers (illegal unless the breaker is designed for it, e.g. Square D Homeline); 9) missing filler plates; 10) not torquing to spec (torque screwdriver); bonus: rat's-nest wiring.
brief: Most of these faults are visible only with the dead-front off, which exposes service conductors and lugs that stay live even with the main breaker off, so homeowner checks are visual and opening the panel is a licensed electrician's job. 1) Double-tapped breakers: two wires under a terminal made for one; a few breakers, such as some Square D models, are labelled for two conductors. 2) Breaker too large for the wire: copper 14 AWG is protected at 15 A, 12 AWG at 20 A, 10 AWG at 30 A (NEC 240.4(D)); the breaker protects the wire, and an upsized one lets it overheat. 3) Wrong-brand breakers: the panel label lists the breakers approved for it, plus any UL Classified breakers listed for that panel; others may seat poorly on the bus and arc. 4) Neutrals and grounds together in a subpanel: they bond only at the service disconnect (NEC 250.24(A)(5)); otherwise neutral current flows on ground wires and metal. 5) Open slots and knockouts: unused breaker openings must be closed with identified filler plates (NEC 408.7), and cables enter through clamps or bushings, not bare knockout edges. 6) Several neutrals under one terminal: each neutral needs its own terminal (NEC 408.41). 7) Missing or wrong cover screws: pointed sheet-metal or drywall screws can pierce wires behind the cover, unlike the maker's blunt screws. 8) Unlabelled or vague circuit directories. 9) Over-stripped or loose conductors: bare copper outside a lug, or terminals below their labelled torque, which NEC 110.14(D) requires reaching by an approved means. 10) Known problem panels: Federal Pacific Stab-Lok, linked by independent testing to breakers that fail to trip (CPSC's early-1980s investigation closed without a recall), and Zinsco, whose breakers can fuse to the aluminum bus; both are routinely flagged by inspectors. Local code may differ.
sources: https://forums.mikeholt.com/threads/classified-cutler-hammer-replacement-breakers-in-different-brand-of-panels.125709/latest — UL Classified breakers for specified panels; panel labels name the maker's breakers

doubts: NEC 240.4(D) values (15/20/30 A) are from standard knowledge, not re-checked in a source this round. The circuit directory rule is usually NEC 408.4(A); not verified, so no number is given. FPE: CPSC closed its investigation without a recall; failure-to-trip percentages (25-50%+) come from secondary sources, so the brief gives no figure. Zinsco 'fuse to the bus' comes from contractor and inspector sources. Reference points I dropped or folded in: panel 'overloading' / 80% rule (it mixes up the load calculation with the breaker total), the cut main ground, twisted grounds, re-marking a white wire used as a hot (my 10 are the operator's list), rat's-nest wiring. Bushings are folded into item 5. 'Double tap' rules depend on the breaker's label; that is stated generally.

title: 9 Electrical Things Every Homeowner Wishes They'd Learned Sooner
reference_points: LRN2DIY (9hlo87E_GdQ), countdown: 5) replace twist-on wire nuts with lever nuts (visible positive clamp, several wires and gauges, reusable); 4) splice a cut wire with a twisted 'knot' splice and heat-shrink (melted with a lighter); 3) replace a damaged plug end instead of the whole cord (brown/blue/green cord colors; brass hot, silver neutral, green ground; tighten the cord clamp); 2) hook the wire clockwise ('with the grain'), worse with stranded wire, use fork terminals for stranded; 1) universal/self-adjusting wire strippers.
brief: Nine everyday electrical basics. 1) The main shutoff is the main breaker in the panel, or a separate disconnect near the meter, and a legible panel directory saves time. 2) A breaker trips from an overload, a short circuit or a ground or arc fault; one reset is normal, repeated trips point to a fault or an overloaded circuit, and a breaker is never upsized, because it is sized to protect the wire (14 AWG copper at 15 A, 12 AWG at 20 A). 3) CPSC recommends testing every GFCI monthly: TEST should cut power to a plugged-in lamp and RESET restore it, and a 'dead' bathroom or garage outlet is often fed through a tripped GFCI elsewhere. 4) A non-contact voltage tester can miss voltage in armored or shielded cable, inside metal boxes or with a weak battery; it is checked on a known live outlet before and after, and silence never proves a wire is dead. 5) Warm, discolored, buzzing or burning-smelling outlets and switches, and flickering lights, point to loose connections or overloads that can arc and overheat. 6) Extension cords are temporary: NEC 400.12 bars cords as a substitute for fixed wiring, run through walls, ceilings, doorways or windows, or fastened to surfaces. 7) Homes wired roughly 1965-1973 may have aluminum branch wiring, which CPSC links to overheating connections; CPSC-recognized repairs (COPALUM, AlumiConn) are a licensed electrician's job. 8) A three-prong outlet doesn't prove a ground; a plug-in tester reveals open grounds and reversed polarity. 9) Good connections: wire loops go clockwise under screws, listed lever connectors accept mixed solid and stranded wire, splices stay inside boxes, and a damaged cord plug can be replaced with a listed plug wired brass-hot, silver-neutral, green-ground. Power is off at the breaker and verified dead before any work.
sources: https://www.cpsc.gov/zh-CN/Recalls/1988/challenger-electrical-equipment-corp-offers-replacement-program-for-9000-gfci-circuit — CPSC: test all GFCIs at least monthly with the test button

doubts: Left out on purpose: the reference's twisted-knot splice with heat-shrink melted by a lighter. It is not an acceptable splice for building wiring (splices belong in boxes with listed connectors); I believe this is NEC 300.15 but did not verify it, so the brief has no number. Universal wire strippers (the reference's #1) are a tool tip, not knowledge, and were left out. The lever connector point should name only listed products (e.g. Wago 221); I did not verify Wago's ratings this round. 'Main disconnect near the meter' reflects newer homes (2020 NEC outdoor emergency disconnect); I did not verify the article number, so none is given. 240.4(D) values are from standard knowledge.

title: Why Exactly Do Electric Plugs Have Holes?
reference_points: Silver Cymbal (Db-dt5U3MCc, ~3 min): 1960s plug has holes; Hubbell 1913 universal plug had indentations that held the plug in; copiers switched to holes; Hubbell sued and lost because the court wanted a standard plug (unverified); modern outlets have nothing that engages the holes; myths: lockout (lockout tags not until late 1950s), saving metal for the war; ANSI says holes are optional; holes stay because customers expect them. Technology Connections (udNXMAflbU8, 20 min): plugging in by feel finds no detent; teardown of four receptacle types finds friction-fit contacts, nothing designed to catch the hole; witness marks run past the hole; holeless plugs fit fine; NEMA drawing says the hole is 'optional and intended for manufacturing purposes only' but must be located per the dimensions; factory alignment rods through the holes when overmolding; polarized plugs explained (wide neutral, lamp shell neutral, switched hot); worn receptacles that barely grip should be replaced.
brief: The holes in US plug blades come from the earliest plug designs and survive mainly for manufacturing. Harvey Hubbell's 1904 separable plug patent used flat blades set in tandem; his 1912 patent turned them parallel, the layout behind today's NEMA 1-15 plug. Early designs used indentations or holes that matched spring bumps in the receptacle so the plug engaged firmly. Modern receptacle contacts mostly grip the blade by spring pressure and friction, and the hole sits forward of where the contacts touch on a fully inserted plug, which is why plugs without holes fit just as snugly. The NEMA dimension drawing states the hole is optional and intended for manufacturing purposes only, but if used must be located where shown. In the factory, alignment rods threaded through the holes hold the blades in position while the plug body is molded around them, and the holes also take shipping seals and some lockout devices. Claims that the holes save metal or date from wartime rationing don't fit: holes appear decades before World War II and the metal saved is trivial. On a polarized two-prong (NEMA 1-15) plug the wider blade is neutral, so a lamp's screw shell and a switched appliance stay on the neutral side and the switch breaks the hot. A NEMA 5-15 plug adds a round or U-shaped ground pin, longer than the blades so it connects first and disconnects last; that pin also fixes the orientation, so the blades are often both narrow. In the code, '1' means two-wire non-grounding, '5' means 125 V grounding, and '15' is the amp rating. Tamper-resistant receptacles, required in dwellings since the 2008 NEC (now 406.12), have shutters that open only when both blades push at once. A receptacle that barely grips a plug has worn contacts that can overheat.
sources: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=udNXMAflbU8 — Technology Connections transcript (NexLev): NEMA 'optional ... manufacturing purposes only', receptacle contact teardown, alignment rods, polarization

doubts: Silver Cymbal's claims that Hubbell sued the copiers, lost, and that the court ruled for a standard plug were not verified and are left out; his '1913' date conflicts with the 1904/1912 patent dates. 'Holes take shipping seals and lockout devices' is reported by secondary sources (HowStuffWorks/Mental Floss), not a manufacturer. The 2008 NEC start for tamper-resistant receptacles is from standard knowledge (sources found only showed the 2011 text). The ground pin being longer is from the NEMA standard as commonly described; I did not check the dimension drawing. The meaning of NEMA '1'/'5' is from standard knowledge. The title says 'exactly'; the honest answer is that there is no single modern purpose, which the brief says.

title: Why Do LED Bulbs Glow After You Switch Them Off? (WARNING)
reference_points: ElectroBOOM (_bgUy6zA0ts, 10 min; companion to Steve Mould): some LED bulbs glow faintly when switched off; touching one terminal with the bulb on the hot makes it glow through body capacitance; microamp currents (about 2-140 uA) make it glow; LEDs in series have a threshold (~70-90 V); cheap bulb teardown: capacitive-dropper driver (two 0.68 uF caps, 1 Mohm bleeder, bridge rectifier, two strings of 32 LEDs, 100 ohm resistors); stray capacitance between the hot and the switched wire in house wiring leaks enough current with the switch off; fix: a resistor (~470 kohm) across the rectifier output, or a second 'proper' LED/incandescent bulb in parallel; switching-driver bulbs need milliamps to start, so they stay dark.
brief: An LED bulb glows faintly when off because a tiny current still reaches it, from four usual sources. 1) Capacitive coupling: the switch leg, the wire from the switch to the fixture, often runs beside the always-hot conductor in the same cable, and the two act as a small capacitor. With the switch open, alternating current still couples across in microamps, and long runs and three-way travelers couple more. 2) Lighted switches that glow when off pass a small current through the bulb to power their own indicator; Pass & Seymour states its illuminated switches may make LED and CFL bulbs glow or flicker when off. 3) Dimmers and smart switches wired without a neutral draw standby current through the bulb; NEC 404.2(C) requires a neutral at most switch locations that control lighting. 4) The dangerous case: a switch wired on the neutral instead of the hot, which NEC 404.2(B) forbids; the fixture, socket and bulb base stay at 120 V while it is off, a shock risk when a bulb is changed. Cheap LED bulbs often use a capacitive-dropper driver feeding long strings of series LEDs, which light on microamps, while incandescents need far more current, and bulbs with switching drivers need milliamps to start. Fixes: the switch moved to the hot conductor, by an electrician; a standard switch, or an LED-rated lighted switch, in place of an old lighted one; a smart switch that uses a neutral; dimmable LEDs from the dimmer maker's compatibility list; or a load capacitor such as Lutron's LUT-MLC, wired at the fixture. Glow with flicker, buzzing or warm devices points to a loose connection, a job for a licensed electrician. Power is off at the breaker and verified dead before work; local code may differ.
sources: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_bgUy6zA0ts — ElectroBOOM transcript (first 3.5 min, NexLev) plus NexLev video watch of 3:20-10:26: capacitive-dropper driver, stray capacitance, switching drivers immune

doubts: Neutral-less smart switches mostly leak through the load (bulb) and some through the ground wire; the brief says through the bulb, which is the glow-causing path. ElectroBOOM's own fixes (a resistor soldered inside the bulb, or a bulb in parallel) are left out: the first is not a homeowner fix, the second only works in multi-lamp fixtures. The LUT-MLC is meant for Lutron controls; with other brands results vary (forum reports). 'WARNING' is backed by the switched-neutral case. The glow from coupling itself is not a stated hazard in any source. A 404.2(C) exception covers replacement switches where a neutral cannot be added without removing finishes.
